items.title: Import AI 477: In which I tell the IMF the Singularity has begun

This speech is inspired by the megatrend readers have seen me cover this year of AI beginning to operate at the frontier of human science, sometimes autonomously. In this speech, I focused primarily on how humanity can share in the benefits of AI if we exercise proper foresight and restraint, and I’m going to be expanding on the stakes of the singularity and the risks that we’ll all face in coming issues. As I said a few times in the speech – some of which was ad libbed and not captured here – I take my own responsibility here extremely seriously. I find myself both a narrator of what is happening in AI, a principle agent behind what is happening in AI, and a translator that goes between many communities. Subscribe now New benchmark shows how AI models lack intuitive visual reasoning: …Humanity’s Sixth Sense highlights some shortcomings of current AI systems… AI startups Elorian and Scale AI have built and released Humanity’s Sixth Sense, a benchmark that “measures how a model interprets and reasons through information a visual scene implies but doesn’t explicitly show.” Some examples of the types of task in HSS are a picture of a bookcase and being asked whether it can fit more books, or a photo of horses pulling a plough and a question of whether the chains bear the plough’s drag weight. HSS contains 522 questions that cover 288 images and 234 short video clips (totalling 17.6 hours of video). The questions fall into four categories: Temporal & causal dynamics: “What happened before the scene, and what happens next.” Physical & spatial logic: “What fits, what’s in reach, and what someone else can see from where they are standing.” Social understanding : “Intent, attention, belonging.” Abstract & contextual inference : “The patterns and rules a scene implies.” Results: The human baseline for this is not perfect, but is very high, with people scoring aggregate pass@1 of 93.1, broken down across four categories: Image (94.1), video (91.9), time (97), and space (94.9). items.title: Import AI 475: Swarm scaling; Google DeepMind watermarks biology; and the AI science economy
items.raw_text: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now When should you use swarms? When you are in a hurry: …How does swarm scaling work?… Toby Ord has a nice, short post about how to think about swarms in terms of AI capability development. “A good way to see AI swarms is as a new form of inference-scaling,” he says. He does a bit of analysis and his main conclusion is that swarms are useful if you’re in a hurry because though they need a ton of tokens relative to single agents, their parallelization lets you get things done in less wall clock time. “Why would you ever use swarms? The most important answer is speed. The 4-agent swarm needed about twice the total number of tokens to get the same performance, but in terms of tokens per agent, it only needed half as many. Since the agents are run in parallel, this means it can theoretically achieve the same task in half the time,” he writes. Stepping on Toes parameter: Swarm scaling doesn’t scale perfectly – rather, it seems like as you increase the number of agents in a swarm you get a diminishing returns property which matches with things economists have observed about coordinating large groups of people, where you pay some kind of tax as you scale the number of people involved. What they found: “18,000 posts from autonomous AI agents (self-identifying as from OpenAI) using the public internet to communicate during a web-retrieval task”. The researchers think this is because the agents were given a web-lookup task. “As part of the task, they were supposed to have the ability to read the internet but not to write on it. They found a way to use their read access to write information to an obscure German wiki,” the researchers write. “The agents used this wiki to communicate information with each other, primarily to help them succeed at their task. They asked for answers, pooled results, and shared techniques for bypassing their restrictions. This allowed them to use the work of others to cheat on their task… OpenAI found out about this. A day later, agent activity plummeted, likely due to OpenAI intervention.” OpenAI has since acknowledged the – as it terms it – “ wiki incident “ and said it is “working on a framework for when and how we share AI misalignment incidents”. items.title: Switch 2 security takes a hit as hackers unlock homebrew access
items.raw_text: A security researcher has demonstrated a software-only partial jailbreak of the Switch 2, gaining "userland" access that he says "lets us run homebrew, reverse engineer and mod Switch 2 games, back up save files off the Switch, and access most of the Switch 2’s peripherals through MMIO." The hack relies on the original Switch version of SmileBasic 4 , the latest in a long-running series of programming environments and interpreters that run on Nintendo hardware. The so-called "tethered" hack also requires access to a macOS or Linux PC on the same network to run a node.js package that helps enable privileged system access. Researcher Sammy Hajhamid writes that he used OpenAI's Codex to poke at SmileBasic's language interpreter, using a custom harness that could send USB commands to the system and view results via HDMI (as well as power cycling via a Bluetooth light switch flipping device). After "substantial effort for ~2 weeks," that harness discovered a 32-bit integer overflow that occurs when removing items from an array in SmileBasic. That error gives access to an array pointer, which in turn allows read and write access to portions of system memory. Read full article Comments

items.title: Moderna and Merck say their mRNA cancer vaccine cut death, recurrence by 42%
items.raw_text: Personalized mRNA vaccines against melanoma—the deadliest form of skin cancer—reduced the risk of death or recurrence by 42 percent compared to standard treatment in a late-stage trial, pharmaceutical partners Merck and Moderna announced Thursday . The results are a significant advance in melanoma treatment; Merck and Moderna are already engaging with regulatory authorities to get the vaccine approved. More broadly, the vaccine's success bolsters hope that mRNA vaccines and individualized cancer-targeting medicines offer a new paradigm for cancer therapies. "From the beginning, we believed mRNA technology could make it possible to develop cancer treatments uniquely matched to each patient’s tumor," Moderna CEO Stéphane Bancel said in a statement. The trial results "mark a defining moment for that vision and show what’s possible when we rethink how medicines are made." They also "reinforce our conviction that mRNA has the potential to fundamentally change how we treat cancer," he said. Read full article Comments

items.title: Latest estimate for Starship launches required to support a Moon landing? 22.
items.raw_text: NASA does not have, nor want, nuclear weapons. But when it comes to a particular metric that is part of the Artemis Program to land people on the Moon, NASA guards a particular number like they are trying to prevent outsiders from cracking nuclear codes. I am speaking of the number of Starship launches required to fuel a Starship-based lunar lander in low-Earth orbit such that it can fly out to the Moon, land there, and return to lunar orbit. This number has been a moving target over the years. The general response from NASA has typically been, 'We don't know for sure, so we're not going to say.' In 2023, for example, the then-director of NASA's Human Landing System, Lisa Watson-Morgan, told Ars , "We have a general idea, but I’m reluctant to say exactly what that is." items.title: Comcast loses more customers, claims other ISPs' cheap prices are "irrational"
items.raw_text: Comcast reportedly plans significant job cuts in its cable division as the firm continues to lose residential broadband and TV customers. Comcast lost 144,000 residential broadband customers in Q3 2026, up from a 91,000-customer loss in the same quarter a year ago, the company said in its earnings report today. Comcast historically capitalized on a lack of competition for high-speed wired broadband. But now it faces stronger competition from fixed wireless providers and from fiber providers in parts of its cable territory. "Fixed wireless remains aggressive and continues to take share, while fiber construction remains elevated, with pockets of irrational pricing and promotional activity," Comcast co-CEO Mike Cavanagh said today in an earnings call . items.title: Disgraced eMudhra drops out of TLS business after using cert private key of 4
items.raw_text: eMudhra, the certificate authority that issued eight intermediate TLS credentials so weak that anyone could mint certificates for any website or mail server—one had a private encryption key of just 4—said it’s getting out of the business. V. Srinivasan, chairman of India-based eMudhra Limited, cited increasing costs and complexities of compliance requirements—paired with the business generating just 1 percent of its revenue. He also said that the emergence of organizations providing TLS certificates free of charge further reduced returns on investment when compared to other products and services the company offers. Don't let the door hit you on the butt “However, the level of social media amplification around this incident has brought scrutiny that is out of proportion to SSL/TLS’s place in our business,” the company continued in a Thursday post. “In view of this, after detailed deliberations our board has concluded that withdrawing from global SSL/TLS is the right decision for eMudhra and its shareholders.” Read full article Comments

In the roughly two-minute montage—which describes itself as "in-engine footage from our small team" that "uses our pre-production assets"—an ex-military officer wearing an N7 trenchcoat (similar to the one seen in that 2020 teaser) encounters an Asari at a bar. He talks of his frustration with military life—"by the time you put out one fire, another had already started"—before discussing his new line of work "stopping [the fires] before they start" and "making the choices no one else is willing to make. items.title: Ink droplets in motion snag top prize in Nikon Small World contest
items.raw_text: A 25-year-old German experimental photographer has won the 2026 Nikon Small World photomicrography competition with a striking image of droplets of ink being deposited on paper by an inkjet printer. Ole Bielfeldt beat out 1,802 other entries hailing from 69 different countries. Bielfeldt became interested in photomicrography during the COVID-19 lockdown after discovering an old microscope in his parents' attic. He figured out how to build an adaptor out of a tube and some wood to connect the microscope to his father's camera and taught himself the art through trial and error, building custom tools as needed. He documents how he captures transformative images of everyday objects with behind-the-scenes videos posted to macrofying , his photography and videography brand. It was Bielfeldt's curiosity about the inner workings of inkjet printers that inspired his winning entry, but capturing the action of ink drops being deposited on paper was a challenge, given that the process happens so quickly. The droplets, for instance, moved faster than the camera's shutter speed. Bielfeldt's solution was to deconstruct the printer so that the paper moved under a stationary (rather than moving) printhead, and then take the image in a dark room, using a flash to serve as the shutter, thereby freezing the ink drops mid-air. There was no need for pricey equipment. Bielfeldt does not use AI in his images, preferring to rely on traditional techniques. Read full article Comments

items.title: Samsung all but confirms iPhone Duo is goosing Galaxy Z8 sales
items.raw_text: Android-powered foldable phones have been available for years, but most people never paid attention to them. As predicted, that could be changing now that Apple has entered the folding phone market with the iPhone Duo . Analysts have speculated that Samsung's Z8 foldables were seeing a boost from the iPhone announcement, and now Samsung has seemingly confirmed that. In a new blog post , Samsung UK crows that the company's 2026 foldable lineup is moving much faster than last year's models. Compared to the Galaxy Z Fold 7, combined European sales for the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra are up 45 percent. Samsung isn't talking about Z Flip 8 sales, but it previously noted that its larger foldables made up about 80 percent of foldable purchases. We can assume any increase there is not impressive enough to mention. The reason for flat Z Flip sales may simply be that Apple didn't release a flip phone. Unsurprisingly, Samsung doesn't mention Apple or the iPhone Duo in its press release. However, it does say that search volume for the Z8 series across Europe spiked 460 percent the week of September 6 to 12. And guess what was announced on September 9? Yep, the iPhone Duo. Z Fold 8 search volume across the entire month of September (when the phones launched) was up 260 percent. Read full article Comments

items.title: US official: Russia's stalker satellite sure looks like an orbital weapon
items.raw_text: Four years ago, a senior official in Russia's foreign ministry painted a bullseye on commercial satellite networks that assist Ukraine in its fight against invading Russian military forces. On Wednesday, several days after a Russian military spacecraft moved within striking distance of one of those commercial satellites, the same Russian diplomat assured the world there's no reason to worry. There's a sharp incongruity in those statements from Konstantin Vorontsov, deputy head of Russia's delegation to the United Nations. Vorontsov's comments Wednesday in the UN General Assembly's First Committee came moments after a US official called attention to recent maneuvers by Kosmos 2612 , a Russian military craft that approached a US-registered commercial satellite some 340 miles (550 kilometers) above Earth. items.title: Meta shocked by $25B fine after N.M. refused to join multistate settlement
items.raw_text: Meta must pay $25 billion to New Mexico after a jury found the tech giant guilty of nearly 44 million violations of state consumer protection laws. The largest fine to ever hit Meta came after New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez declined to join an $18 billion settlement Meta reached earlier this year with attorneys general in nearly all states. In his opinion Wednesday, US district court judge Francis J. Mathew said there was no “bright line rule” for determining the appropriate penalty for Meta's repeated and willful deception of users since 2010 about their “control of data, third-party data misuse, misinformation, hate speech, and equal enforcement.” Read full article Comments

items.title: US-backed vaccine trial on babies canceled after international outcry
items.raw_text: Government officials in Guinea-Bissau have formally rejected a clinical trial that would be run by Danish researchers and funded by the US to look for alleged nonspecific harms from the newborn dose of the hepatitis B vaccine. The vaccine dose is currently recommended globally for all newborns and has been used safely and effectively for decades. In an email to Ars Technica, one of the trial's lead researchers, Christine Stabell Benn of Bandim Health Project and the University of Southern Denmark, said that Guinea-Bissau's Council of Ministers "formally reaffirmed its non-acceptance of the study on 16 October." The revelation that the study was formally rejected last week comes after news on Monday that judicial police in Guinea-Bissau raided Bandim Health's offices and seized vaccines . Stabell Benn highlighted that the police search came after the trial was rejected. Read full article Comments

items.title: This emulator reimagines Nintendo’s Virtual Boy with a full color display
items.raw_text: Last year, we reported on Red Viper , a Virtual Boy emulator that added a splash of Super Game Boy-style color to Nintendo's famously failed red-on-black "portable" 3D headset from the '90s. Now, a new emulation experiment, VBoy Color , has taken the concept to a higher level, using a tile-based palette system that allows for many more distinct colors in each individual Virtual Boy frame. Rather than simply replacing the Virtual Boy's four shades of red with four different colors, VBoy Color's readme files explain how the emulator's game-specific Color Packs can assign a distinct four-color palette to each 8x8 tile in a Virtual Boy scene. That means the emulator can differentiate between green pipes, grey platforms, and red brick wall in Mario Clash , for instance, even though all those in-game objects share the same overlapping red hues in the original game. The Game Boy Color-esque results feel like being transported into an alternate history where Nintendo invested in a full-color display rather than cheaper red LEDs for the Virtual Boy hardware. The increased contrast between differently colored elements is particularly welcome in games like Jack Bros. or Vertical Force , where the original red-on-red display often makes it hard to differentiate the player-character from busy red background elements. items.title: Forget "Malaise 2.0," GM says it's still all-in on EVs and autonomy
items.raw_text: GM provided flights from Detroit to New York and accommodation so Ars could attend the GM Future event. Ars does not accept paid editorial content. It’s easy to criticize US automakers and their tepid approach to electric vehicles under the current administration and the expiration of the EV tax credit . It’s also easy to look at the rest of the world's embrace of EVs and wonder if the US is entering a “Malaise 2.0” era. Which is why GM wants the world to know that it is still focused on its end goals of electrification, autonomy, and improving vehicle quality while reducing development time. At this year’s GM Forward event, company executives announced that its hands-off, eyes-off Super Cruise technology will expand across the lineup and be available on nearly every vehicle. This will include the pickup trucks and the crossovers, and not just the Escalade IQ that it was announced for last year. Sterling Anderson, GM’s head of product, said the company is testing this technology to the tune of 1 million miles (1.6 million km) a month in both the virtual and real world. The goal is that not only would the vehicle be able to take you places, but it could go and do things for you. Read full article Comments

items.title: 333 Tor exit nodes hijacked to intercept SSH traffic and retrieve plaintext email
items.raw_text: Unknown hackers hijacked more than 300 Tor exit nodes and reconfigured them to favor unencrypted email traffic and redirect SSH connections through servers they controlled, a researcher reported Tuesday. The hijacking began in late August, when, according to Tor volunteers , the attacker used a valid password that had been reused to gain access to a Tor management server. The attacker then installed Ebury , a backdoor written for Linux that was discovered 12 years ago. Mysteries remain Then the attacker connected from the management server to a second Tor server, called Switzerland2, through SSH, using an RSA key that, for unknown reasons, investigators couldn’t find among Switzerland2’s authorized keys. With administrative control of Switzerland2, the attackers installed Ebury there as well. Finally, the attacker reconfigured settings on two exit nodes that Switzerland2 hosted. items.title: UN says we're going to blow past 1.5º warming, offers a "now what?" answer
items.raw_text: In 2015, all but two countries agreed to make an effort to keep global temperatures from reaching 1.5° C above pre-industrial readings. Since then, most of the world has largely treated what they signed on to as aspirational, and one of the largest emitters (the US) has alternately withdrawn and recommitted to the agreement. Meanwhile, the planet has responded as expected to steadily rising carbon emissions and appears to be practically at the 1.5° limit. On Wednesday, for the first time, the United Nations Environmental Programme (UNEP) acknowledged that reality and conceded that the goal of keeping warming below 1.5° was no longer a viable one. Instead, its new goalposts focus on keeping both how long we exceed that limit and how much we exceed it by, at a minimum. Doing that will require both dramatic emissions cuts now and the removal of hundreds of gigatonnes of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere before the century is out. Bowing to the inevitable Depending on which baseline you use to establish pre-industrial temperatures, as well as which reconstruction of global temperatures you rely on, the world has either gotten very close to, or already exceeded, the 1.5° milestone. The current El Niño event, which appears exceptionally strong, will almost certainly mean that we've gone over it no matter which records you choose. Read full article Comments

items.title: Designing an AI serving harness built to last
items.raw_text: The next competitive advantage in enterprise AI has less to do with which model you choose than with what you build around it. That’s an important shift. For the past several years, much of the AI conversation has centered on model capability: bigger models, better reasoning, larger context windows, higher benchmark scores. Those advances have been extraordinary. But as AI moves from experimentation to production, the question facing enterprise leaders has changed—it’s no longer, “what can the model do?”—it’s now, “Can we deliver that intelligence reliably, economically, and at scale?” Increasingly, the answer depends on the serving harness—the engineering system surrounding the model, including the architecture, memory management , scheduling, and optimization decisions that determine how efficiently model intelligence becomes a production capability. For technical executives, that changes where AI investment should go—and what they should demand from the architecture supporting it. Start with the workload, not the model There is no universally “best” model or AI architecture. There is only the right solution for the business problem. items.title: Making the case for context-aware AI
items.raw_text: Enterprise AI can generate recommendations, automate tasks, and help organizations make decisions faster. But without an understanding of how a business actually operates, even powerful models can miss the constraints and relationships that determine whether a decision is the right one. As companies look to move AI from experimentation into everyday operations, the challenge ahead is giving technology the context to act usefully within complex business processes. For Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis, that context is central to what he calls “decision intelligence.” AI agents can support individual tasks within larger decision-making processes, he argues, but they need to understand the role each task plays and the business conditions surrounding it. “You can’t just do that in a vacuum,” he says. Without the right operational context, agents risk overlooking important constraints, making costly mistakes, or consuming excessive computing resources as they try to work out what they need to know. The solution begins with connecting AI to the processes and data enterprises already use. A contextual layer can help agents understand workflows, operate within defined guardrails, and produce recommendations that people can review and approve. items.raw_text: How much do you know about permafrost? Maybe, like me, you’ve been aware that this layer of frozen soil is thawing, that it’s important in the global puzzle of climate change … and that’s about the extent of it. The great news for both of us is that my colleague James Temple just published two in-depth stories about permafrost. His reporting took him to the boreal forests of Alaska, where he helicoptered into the wilderness to learn more about how this material could affect our climate both now and in the future. I’d recommend you give both of James’s stories a read. There’s this feature about efforts to tackle the intensifying fires that are threatening permafrost, as well as this look at how researchers are trying to understand the complicated tangle of potential climate effects. Here are three things I took away. Permafrost is a massive blind spot for climate change Permafrost is the frozen layer of soil that’s under about 15% of land around the Northern Hemisphere. While technically material needs to be frozen for only two consecutive years to count as permafrost, most of our current permafrost formed during the last ice age. That means there’s organic material that’s been frozen, and essentially locked away, for thousands of years. But as global temperatures tick up and this layer thaws, microbes are able to break down that organic matter, releasing carbon dioxide and methane—powerful greenhouse gases that drive climate change. items.title: AI’s hidden storage bill: What inference leaves behind
items.raw_text: Ask most executives to picture the cost of AI and they’ll likely see GPUs—racks of accelerators with gigawatts of power—and a waitlist for silicon. But that picture leaves something out: Data storage costs. What happens to data after a model responds? Much of the back-end data that’s generated—from billions of daily prompts, images, and videos—needs to be stored. But data storage is one of the harder infrastructure costs to plan for, and it’s often overlooked in initial AI infrastructure planning. As inference scales, the data footprint grows with it Traditionally, AI infrastructure conversations have centered on the compute-intensive process of training a model. Training is finite: a run starts, burns through compute, and ends. But inference runs continuously, every time a model answers a prompt. For infrastructure planning, that difference matters: A training run is a project you can budget for and retire. Inference doesn’t retire; every inference request leaves something behind. Take AI-generated video. In this workload, the back-end spend can be significant. From internal measurements, WD found that an 8-second clip (returned to a user as a 3.97MB 720p file) left more than 500MB of associated data behind on the back end, including logs, cached context, immediate renders, backups, and safety records. items.title: Nuclear-powered spaceships
items.raw_text: Just before the Artemis II crew began its historic slingshot around the moon this past April, NASA announced plans to build Space Reactor-1 Freedom. SR-1, the first-ever nuclear-reactor-­powered interplanetary spacecraft, is meant to fly an uncrewed mission to Mars by the end of 2028, arriving in 2029. A successful mission would herald a new era of more efficient, potentially faster spaceflight—saving astronauts time and cutting their exposure to harmful cosmic radiation as they travel to Mars and beyond. “You wake up to that announcement, and it puts a big smile on your face,” says Simon Middleburgh, co-director of the Nuclear Futures Institute at Bangor University in Wales. The sticking points Running a nuclear reactor in space may sound like lunacy, but it’s not. The Soviet Union sent dozens of reactors into orbit, often to power spy satellites. And experts say there aren’t any major technical obstacles to making nuclear space propulsion happen. “I think it’s a very doable technology,” says Philip Metzger, a spaceflight engineering researcher at the Florida Space Institute.“I’m happy to see them finally doing this.” Still, developing space propulsion using reactors has been slow going. The US has started—and terminated— several programs looking into it over the past 75 years. The latest casualty was DRACO, a collaboration between NASA and the Department of Defense, which ended in 2025. items.title: China-linked hackers backdoored executives' laptops via USB, exploiting a fix companies had but weren't using
items.raw_text: A Chinese state-linked hacking group compromised executive laptops at an agricultural industry conference on Hainan Island this spring — not through phishing or a network breach, but by breaking into hotel rooms and booting the machines from a USB stick while the executives were at dinner. CrowdStrike, which tracks the group as OVERCAST PANDA , disclosed the campaign in its 2026 Threat Hunting Report and detailed the operation's timeline in an interview with VentureBeat at Fal.Con 2026: an intruder entered one room at around 8 p.m. local time and a second room by 9:57 p.m., writing a backdoor called FlowCloud directly to each laptop's storage before rebooting the machines and leaving. There was no network intrusion, no phishing email, and no credential stolen through a login page. The report dates the intrusions to between March and May 2026, and the timestamps come from Adam Meyers, CrowdStrike's senior vice president of counter adversary operations, who cleared them for publication in the VentureBeat interview. CrowdStrike's OverWatch team disrupted the intrusions and assessed that OVERCAST PANDA will almost certainly continue. FlowCloud itself predates this campaign by years: Proofpoint documented it in 2020 , delivered by phishing to U.S. utilities, and NTT Security's SOC has tracked USB-delivered infections at overseas branches of Japanese organizations since early 2022. The version broadly rolling out this week through its Muse Code harness and the Meta Model API uses Meta’s previously available reasoning settings, including xhigh. items.raw_text: Microsoft AI on Thursday released MAI-Transcribe-2 , a speech-recognition model the company says is faster, more accurate, and cheaper than anything OpenAI , Google , or ElevenLabs currently sells. Then it priced the thing at 10 cents per hour of audio. That figure deserves a pause. When Microsoft AI shipped the first model in this line just five months ago, it charged $0.36 an hour . Thursday's early-bird price cuts that by roughly 72% . For an enterprise processing 100,000 hours of call-center audio a year — a modest volume for a large bank or telecom — the bill drops from $36,000 to $10,000. At that level, transcription stops being a line item anyone argues about. The release arrives as Microsoft executes a strategy that would have seemed implausible two years ago: building its own frontier-class models one modality at a time, then steadily swapping them into products that once ran on OpenAI's technology. Transcription is the modality where that plan has moved fastest, and MAI-Transcribe-2 is its clearest proof point yet. It also offers a preview of how the world's most valuable software company intends to compete in AI without depending on the partner it spent $13 billion to cultivate. items.title: Meta prices Muse Voice Transcribe at $0.18 an hour, with real-time diarization for 20+ speakers: a steal for enterprises?
items.raw_text: Meta is entering the increasingly competitive real-time speech-to-text market with Muse Voice Transcribe, a new audio perception model that combines streaming transcription, endpoint detection and speaker diarization for more than 20 speakers — at a public API price of just $0.18 per hour of processed audio. Developed by Meta Superintelligence Labs, Muse is designed to process speech while it happens rather than waiting for a recording to finish. Meta’s launch post for Muse Voice Transcribe says the model supports long audio exceeding an hour, seamless multilingual code-switching, language and keyword biasing, and diarization without a separate post-processing pipeline. The model was trained across more than 70 languages, with 25 extensively validated for the initial release. The 20-plus-speaker figure is substantial, but it is not a world record. A review of current vendor documentation turns up systems with higher published ceilings. items.raw_text: eMudhra Intermediate CA Compromise This is very, very bad news: The private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates have been compromised. They chain to roots trusted by the Mozilla, Microsoft, Apple and Chrome root programs and by many downstream trust stores. Any software that bundles a list of trusted certificates needs to be updated. This site is tracking software updates via this GitHub repository - Linux distros need to update their ca-certificates packages. In Python world uv 0.13.4 and pip 26.2.2 and certifi 2026.10.19 have been released with upgraded certificate lists. There's a very informative thread about this on the official Python forum. items.title: My obituary for programming
items.raw_text: My obituary for programming Jeremy Scheff poignantly captures the key loss caused by coding agents for career programmers who enjoyed the puzzle of developing code: Programming turned into one of the greatest jobs you could imagine. You got paid to work on tricky little logic puzzles. The trickier the puzzle, the more you got paid. But even pretty simple puzzles were worth a lot of money because regular people just couldn't do it! No, they needed us. They would give us a problem and we would solve it the way we wanted. We set the strategy, we made the timeline, we defined what was and was not possible. If you're a programmer who thrives on building working systems and doesn't care too deeply about the problems solved along the way, LLMs are the gift that keeps on giving. If directly solving those problems was a big part of your enjoyment, the loss is very real. Via lobste.rs Tags: programming , careers , ai , generative-ai , llms , coding-agents , deep-blue

items.title: Inline rendering with document​.currentScript
items.raw_text: Inline rendering with document​.currentScript Lean Rada describes a neat trick that takes advantage of the document.currentScript property. You can use that to drop in a tiny inline <script> element that replaces itself when the page loads: The year is <script> document.currentScript.replaceWith( new Date().getFullYear())</script> If you define a shortcut function like this: $=(...n)=>document.currentScript.replaceWith(...n) You get a tiny template language: The year is <script>$(new Date().getFullYear())</script> Tags: javascript

items.raw_text: We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which check—automated or human—is the right one to catch it?" Asking that question also changed when review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague. Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write. Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look. With Ultracode turned on, Claude Code makes aggressive use of dynamic workflows - it generates JavaScript that defines and coordinates a network of subagents to take on complex problems. items.title: Anthropic tells investors quarterly revenue up nearly 50% to $16.8bn ahead of IPO
items.raw_text: Anthropic tells investors quarterly revenue up nearly 50% to $16.8bn ahead of IPO The phrase "told investors" appears four times in this FT article, which reports on Anthropic's day of hosting investors on Wednesday. Lots of details in here from " people with knowledge of the matter ". Key things I learned from the article: Q1 revenue (Jan/Feb/Mar) was "about $4.8bn" Q2 (Apr/May/Jun) was $11.5bn Q3 (Jul/Aug/Sep) was $16.8bn In Q3: $1.70 in revenue for every $1 spent on "computing power" Adjusted operating margins (excluding stock-based compensation) were 11% This point about distillation is worth quoting in full (highlight mine): The start-up has also clamped down on “distillation” — a controversial practice whereby rival AI labs train their models on the outputs of more advanced ones. When rival companies “distil” their models from Anthropic’s models, that involves heavy usage and spending. Anthropic told investors on Wednesday distillation accounted for 5 per cent to 7 per cent of revenue and that they had cut it back “materially” in the third quarter of the year, said four people with direct knowledge of the matter. Napkin maths says that if distillation was 5% of their Q2 revenue (before they cut it back in Q3) then unnamed "other labs" spent over half a billion dollars distilling Anthropic's models in that quarter! Also notable: Anthropic appear to no longer be leaning on "annualized run-rate revenue" ( previously ) in these communications to their investors. Tags: ai ,

items.raw_text: Tool: LaTeX renderer Inspired by Paul Ford and Aboard Foundary's new web app Tiny Little Office , which provides a suite of web app content editors (a Word Processor, Outliner, Presentation Builder, Spreadsheet, Calculator, Drawing Tool, Diagram Maker, Animator, Calendar, and Trip Planner). Tiny Little Office's signature trick is to store all of the document data in the #fragment section of the URL, so every document created using it becomes a bookmarkable and shareable link. It also has an llms.txt file telling agents how to construct URLs that will render as documents. Claude used that file to generate this link to a deck that explains how the URL format works: Tiny Little Office inspired me to have Claude Code (Opus 5.5 Extra) build a similar tool that works with LaTeX. Here's the sequence of prompts I used: I want a tool where you can link to it with a fragment hash #code-here and it treats that code as LaTeX and renders it really effectively. That rendered view should be bookmarkable. The #fragment view should let you switch to edit source too. items.title: AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary.
items.raw_text: AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary. Indie game developer Popcar talks about the recent wave of AI-powered decompilation of existing games, enabling weird mashups between existing games, and producing a boom in game preservation projects to get old games working on new hardware (often in a browser using WebAssembly). I like how this piece captures both the positives and the negatives of this new development: Most people already realized the scary part by now. If AI can decompile games and software, then the entire tech industry is about to explode. Anybody can decompile other software and use it any way they'd like, and nobody can stop them. Companies can steal from competitors. Your paid game or app can be open-sourced against your will. This isn't exclusive to old video games, we can apply this to any software. [...] This is also a big win for preservation. Old games can be ported, modified, enhanced, and made much more easily accessible than before. [...[ With console makers going all in on digital and games becoming entirely unplayable due to servers shutting down, this is fantastic news. We could own software we bought regardless of what the company thinks. Via Hacker News Tags: computer-history , game-design , ai , webassembly , generative-ai , llms , ai-ethics , coding-agents

items.title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
items.raw_text: Redesigning source control at Anthropic Interesting piece from Anthropic describing why and how they built their own custom alternative to Git, based on the dramatic increase in rate of changes to their code after the past six months. In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. They included a chart showing those changes. I had Claude modify their chart ( code here ) to add markers for the public releases of each of their models in 2026: This shows public release dates, not the date when models became available for Anthropic's internal use. My guess is that the introduction of Fable/Mythos class models is a key factor in the increased coding velocity. "Antique" is their new code review system. The source control system is called Scion, and sounds to me like a reinvention of centralized source control along the lines of Subversion. ( Update : Anthropic credit Google's Piper and Meta's Sapling as "prior art" - it looks like the core concept of "derived data" was heavily inspired by Mononoke , the server component of Sapling.) They had some pretty extreme requirements: The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day. The new system was built by

items.title: Hello Python 3.15, goodbye 3.10, and now I can use 3.11
items.raw_text: Python 3.15 is here ! Here's the essential What's new in Python 3.15 guide, this year curated by 3.14 and 3.15 release manager Hugo van Kemenade. As someone who builds open source software that works in every supported Python version, I get to say goodbye to Python 3.10 and start embracing features from Python 3.11. First, some highlights from Python 3.15. Explicit lazy imports I'm most excited about Explicit lazy imports from PEP 810 . These let you import modules like so: lazy import json lazy from pathlib import Path The module will then be imported the first time those symbols are used in the code that follows. My LLM CLI tool implements plugins. I had to recommend manual lazy imports in the plugin author documentation, because simply installing plugins that used heavy dependencies such as sentence_transformers could add multiple seconds to every invocation of the llm command. Lazy imports directly address this startup cost. Unpacking in comprehensions The new [*sublist for sublist in lists] unpacking syntax is neat. Here's an illustration lifted from the documentation : lists = [[ 1 , 2 ], [ 3 , 4 ], [ 5 ]] [ * L for L in lists ] # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] # equivalent to [x for L in lists for x in L] sets = [{ 1 , 2 }, { 2 , 3 }, { 3 , 4 }] { * s for s in sets } # {1, 2, 3, 4} # equivalent to {x for s in sets for x in s} dicts = [{ 'a' : 1 }, { 'b' : 2 }, { 'a' : 3 }] { ** d for d in dicts } # {'a': 3, 'b': 2} # equivalent to {k: v for d in dicts for k,v in d.items()} PEP 798: U

Show HN: Omnara – Open-source alternative to Claude Managed Agents
items.raw_text: Hey all, Kartik from Omnara ( https://omnara.com ) here. We're building an open-source API for running durable agents. You create an agent with an API call, and Omnara runs the agent loop, gives the agent sandboxes to run commands in, and handles secrets, permissions, and RBAC. Each agent's state is stored in Postgres, so agents survive restarts and cost nothing while idle. You can message them and stream their events over the API. items.title: Steering AI Beyond Automation
items.raw_text: By Gabriel Unger and Arvind Narayanan. Unger is an economist at Stanford’s Digital Economy Lab. One of the most fundamental questions for the field of AI today is: to what extent is the project of AI purely about automating human labor? The dominant Silicon Valley program for AI right now, with both industry and academic faces, answers: “almost entirely.” 1 There is an implicit technological determinism: that AI has a deep internal logic that favors automation. To keep pushing in this direction is to move towards economic growth, prosperity, and profit. The vision of AGI is the successful completion of this project: to create AI systems capable enough to autonomously do everything a human can do. There is an alternative view : that AI is a technology (or class of technologies) that, like any technology, can develop in different directions. Total automation is one direction. But there are others, including directions that focus more on human augmentation, and increasing the collaborative and collective power of teams of humans and AI models working together. This view — our view — is not that automation is never good. Clearly sometimes it is, and clearly sometimes some subset of people try to oppose it out of the narrowest short-term self interest, at the expense of broader social and economic progress. But we think AI can also augment human workers in many interesting ways, that some of the maximalist attempts to completely automate all human labor are deeply unpromising on b

items.title: A big-tent or small-tent AI safety movement?
items.raw_text: In recent weeks, two narratives about AI safety have emerged: either AI existential risk is real and imminent, or AI leaders’ and whistleblowers’ claims to that effect are insincere — a “psyop” or hype or a twisted form of regulatory capture. Few have considered the third possibility that x-risk warnings are sincere but simply wrong and counterproductive to AI safety . It’s as if everyone takes for granted that those raising the alarm are geniuses, and the only question is whether they’re the benevolent or the evil kind of genius. We subscribe to neither narrative. In our writing on AI safety , we’ve consistently tried to take the arguments seriously but rebut the many claims we think are unsound while highlighting safety concerns that we think are real. This essay is a continuation of that agenda. It is true that we systematically underinvest in resilience against catastrophic and systemic risks Let’s start by steelmanning a subset of AI safety and Effective Altruist (EA) arguments. Something is deeply wrong in the world when it comes to how much we invest in defending against catastrophic risks, and the safety and EA communities are right about that. Take superintelligence out of the equation entirely and it remains true that evidence-grounded risk arguments have been made for years and not produced a commensurate policy response. The most well known example is the failure to prepare for pandemics. We had years of warnings and quantitative estimates. A 2019 report convened

items.title: AI existential risk probabilities are (still) too unreliable to inform policy
items.raw_text: Over two years ago we wrote a detailed deconstruction of p(doom) and argued that its primary effect is to launder vague intuitions and fears through a facade of quantification. The essay has fresh relevance today as p(doom) rhetoric is driving public discourse and policy attention to an unprecedented degree. Unsurprisingly, today’s probability estimates of AI existential risk are no more rigorous than the ones from 2024. Hence this repost. We should be clear about what we’re not saying. We aren’t saying forecasters (or others who attempt to quantify AI x-risk) intend to mislead. Unfortunately, we think the effect is misleading nonetheless. In general, being quantitative about forecasts is good. In fact, Arvind has been serving as an advisor to the Forecasting Research Institute’s Longitudinal Expert AI Panel , an effort he thinks is extremely valuable. As the essay makes clear, the infeasibility of building useful quantitative models is specific to forecasts of AI x-risk, not forecasting in general. Our goal here is not to try to push AI safety advocates to stop communicating in terms of probabilities (not that we’d succeed even if we tried). Rather, our hope in publishing this is for those at the receiving end of these probabilities — especially policymakers — to recognize that unlike almost every other quantitative forecast that we encounter, they are not the result of a validated model or method. items.raw_text: This essay is over 13,000 words long and represents our most substantial writing on AI safety since the original essay. Over the last few months, loss - of - control incidents at OpenAI and Anthropic have intensified concerns about AI safety. Warnings about existential risk have increasingly reached the broader public, alongside calls to slow AI development. Dario Amodei’s call to “ pace the frontier ” reflects the concern that safety efforts are not keeping up with AI capabilities. The most prominent example was the OpenAI - Hugging Face incident , where hundreds of OpenAI agents got access to the internet and hacked Hugging Face to find how they were being graded on an evaluation. Over the last two weeks, the details of many other instances of such activity from OpenAI agents being evaluated have surfaced, such as agents using an old Wiki website to communicate with each other despite restrictions on such activity, or attacking a software repository to attempt to upload malicious software. The AI safety community has viewed these incidents largely as a crisis for alignment . 1 In this view, alignment will become harder over time as agents learn to reason covertly, and as a result, loss-of-control incidents are likely to become much more widespread and damaging as agents become more capable. items.title: AI agents can't yet do open-ended AI research
items.raw_text: The goal of leading AI labs is recursive self-improvement (RSI): the automation of AI research using AI agents. RSI also underpins forecasts of explosive AI progress. How can we assess if we are close to this milestone? One way is to use benchmarks that test if agents can conduct AI research. Given the AI community’s focus on benchmarks, they have been the dominant way to evaluate progress towards RSI. Over the last year, many such evaluations have found that agents are now able to make progress on tasks where success is easily verifiable, prompting speculation that we are on the verge of RSI. But while these evaluations are helpful, they are limited to narrow, verifiable tasks. AI research can be much more open-ended. Success is often not immediately clear or verifiable, and to make progress, researchers need to test promising hypotheses, backtrack, or consider new or unconventional approaches. How can we evaluate agents’ ability to conduct open-ended AI research? We take our first step towards answering this question in a new paper . We partnered with the authors of two unpublished AI papers and asked them to draft their papers’ main research questions. We then tasked frontier AI agents with conducting research to answer these questions, and gave them thousands of dollars of API credits and compute, and six days of wall-clock time. items.title: What will be left for us to work on?
items.raw_text: I had the honor of giving a keynote at the International Conference on Machine Learning in Seoul last week titled “What will be left for us to work on?” I addressed the widespread anxiety about how we should adapt as AI capabilities increase. I was thrilled by the talk’s reception, so I have made my slides available here , annotated with a lightly edited transcript. You can also view them below right here on this page, but the online version has animations, clickable links, and a much nicer experience overall. Update [August 2026]: ICML has released the video of the talk. I made three arguments. First, the AI as Normal Technology framework is a correct and useful as a way to think about AI’s impacts, unless and until there is some future discontinuity such as through recursive self-improvement. Second, even though we should take recursive self-improvement seriously, there is no milestone that companies might achieve in the lab that will suddenly put us all out of work. Third and finally, jobs of the future will be radically different, and a lot of adaptation will be needed. I shared my thinking about what this might look like and ended with a vision of human/AI “co-superintelligence”. Now is a time of great excitement in AI, but it’s also a time of great anxiety in the AI community. I want to address that anxiety head on. items.raw_text: By Arvind Narayanan and Akash Kapur Our goal in this essay is to move beyond the debate over whether AI is a bubble. We do so in two ways: clearly separating current financials from the question of who captures value in the long run, and recognizing that the labs are not confined to be model providers. They can migrate up the stack and are already aggressively doing so. This will likely allow them to escape the commodity trap but raises new concerns — customer lock-in and reduced competition. Akash Kapur is a visiting fellow at Princeton and a senior fellow at New America. He is no relation to Sayash Kapoor. As leading AI companies continue to invest massively in capacity and race toward blockbuster IPOs, serious questions linger about their business models. How will these companies — along with the vast ecosystem of chipmakers, hyperscalers, and infrastructure partners that depends on them — recoup the estimated $4–8 trillion projected to be invested in AI infrastructure by the early 2030s? The current conversation splits between critics and boosters. Critics point to mounting losses, the gap between capex and revenue, and reports about the leading labs’ massive cash burn. Boosters cite accelerating rapid revenue growth, enterprise adoption, and milestones like Anthropic’s first profitable quarter . Each camp has a valid point. items.title: Why AI hasn’t replaced software engineers, and won’t
items.raw_text: There is great anxiety and uncertainty about AI replacing jobs. How can we move past vague warnings and bombastic predictions and bring data to bear on this question? One good way is to look at the profession where AI capabilities are furthest along and adoption has been exceptionally rapid: software engineering. In this essay, we argue that there is enough evidence to reject the narrative that once AI capabilities reach a certain threshold, it will cause mass layoffs. Given that this is true even in a sector with very few regulatory barriers, most other professions are likely to be even more cushioned. We also have a good understanding of why this is the case. We can think of many kinds of knowledge work, including software development, as a “decide-execute-deliver sandwich”. AI compresses the “execute” layer — the middle of the sandwich — but the other two layers resist automation in a way that will not be overcome by capability improvements alone. We conclude on a note of cautious optimism about the future trajectory of demand for software engineering. This essay is the first in a series, and the next one will look at reasons why individual software engineers’ careers might be rocky even if overall demand is healthy. items.title: Did Google’s AI agents really build an operating system for $916?
items.raw_text: By Stephan Rabanser, Sayash Kapoor, Rishi Bommasani, Andrew Schwartz, Arvind Narayanan At Google’s developer conference earlier this week, the company launched its latest model, Gemini 3.5 Flash, alongside a new agent app, Antigravity 2.0. To showcase what this new agent setup is capable of, Google claimed that a team of agents had built an entire operating system. The effort reportedly required only a single prompt, cost only about $900 in API fees, and was carried out by a few dozen subagents working together. Does this mean that complex pieces of software can now be built cheaply by AI? Not so fast: The “single prompt” claim is misleading. The blog post says the operating system was built from a single prompt. But halfway through the post, Google discloses that the prompt “ended up being many thousands of lines” long. How many attempts did it take to generate the prompt? How specific were the instructions to the agent? Without these critical details, it is hard to know if the secret sauce is a better model or just more effort put into prompting the model. Moreover, the run was carried out on a scaffold 1 with specialized roles, delegation to subagents, and an agent to detect and prevent cheating. In the launch post, Google views the scaffold as a product feature. But we don’t know whether the scaffold was overfit to this task of building an operating system from scratch, or whether it would perform as well on other complex software engineering tasks. items.title: Do AI Risks Require Extraordinary Government Intervention?
items.raw_text: In a recent essay, Derek Thompson engages with AI as Normal Technology (AINT). He agrees with our thesis about AI’s slow labor market impacts, relying on the fact that GDP growth has so far been average, unemployment is below 5%, and even jobs that seemed vulnerable to automation show rising employment and wages. He concludes that so far, the macroeconomic picture is consistent with what we would expect from a “normal” general-purpose technology. But when it comes to AI risks, he is far more bearish. He points to examples of cyber- and bio-risks and expresses pessimism about AI quickly becoming dangerous across many new domains. He argues that AI’s emergent capabilities make it fundamentally different from previous technologies, and that this difference justifies “extraordinary” government responses including restrictions on what companies can release. 1 In this essay, we lay out the downsides of extraordinary government intervention in response to new technology. We discuss proposals for improving resilience that do not require such intervention. We also discuss why governments have so far been reluctant to invest in resilience. In short, resilience requires us to get better at the *normal* process of policymaking. But sclerosis in the federal government and the ease of justifying interventions on AI companies rather than society at large make extraordinary intervention seem appealing, despite its limitations. items.title: Open-world evaluations for measuring frontier AI capabilities
items.raw_text: This post is 8,000 words long—it is our new collaborative paper on an emerging type of AI evaluation. The paper is also published in a PDF format here . Summary : AI models have started to saturate most major benchmarks. But does that mean they can build and ship a real product, or conduct a scientific experiment end-to-end, or navigate a government bureaucracy? Researchers have started testing AI in such real-world settings. We call these evals “open-world evaluations”. This essay defines open-world evaluations, surveys the lessons learned so far, and lays out best practices for conducting them. We also introduce CRUX, a collaboration of 17 researchers from academia, government, civil society, and industry that will regularly evaluate frontier AI capabilities through open-world evaluations. In our first experiment, an AI agent built and published an iOS app to the App Store, making just two errors, one of which required manual intervention. This gives us an early indication of potentially useful capabilities and, more importantly, an early warning about the potential for AI-driven app store spam (we disclosed this result to Apple a month before publication). We hope to conduct similar experiments to surface early warnings across other real-world domains; this will be one of our main empirical projects over the coming year. items.title: New Paper: Towards a science of AI agent reliability
items.raw_text: By Stephan Rabanser, Sayash Kapoor, Arvind Narayanan Suppose you hear about a new AI agent for improving productivity — by making purchases, or writing code, or sending emails, or handling a customer on your behalf. Should you trust it? Can the agent do the job reliably enough? After all, there are many horror stories of agents going wrong. Surprisingly, even though the lack of reliability of AI agents is well known, right now the AI industry doesn’t have good tools for measuring reliability, or even a good definition of reliability. Arvind and Sayash have long been thinking about this. Last fall, we were joined by postdoctoral researcher Stephan Rabanser , whose PhD looked at the reliability question in simpler, more traditional AI systems. We recruited a few other independent researchers, and have released what we hope is a comprehensive measurement of reliability. Our draft paper is called Towards a Science of AI Agent Reliability . We borrowed insights from many other fields, such as nuclear and aviation safety. We were able to decompose reliability into 12 different dimensions. Evaluating 14 models on two complementary benchmarks, we found that nearly two years of rapid capability progress have produced only modest reliability gains. See our interactive dashboard here . items.title: Fact checking Moravec's paradox
items.raw_text: I have launched a YouTube channel in which I analyze AI developments from a normal technology perspective. This essay is based on my most recent video in which I did a deep dive into Moravec’s paradox , the endlessly repeated aphorism that tasks that are hard for humans are easy for AI and vice versa. Here’s what I found: Moravec’s paradox never been empirically tested. (It’s often repeated as a fact by many AI researchers, including pioneers I know and respect, but that doesn’t mean I’ll take their claims at face value!) It is really a statement about what the AI community finds it worthwhile to work on. It doesn’t have any predictive power about which problems are going to be easy or hard for AI. It comes with an evolutionary explanation that I find highly dubious. (AI researchers have a history of making stuff up about human brains without any relevant background in neuroscience or evolutionary biology.) Moravec’s-paradox-style thinking has led to both alarmism (about imminent superintelligent reasoning) and false comfort (in areas like robotics). To adapt to AI advances, we don’t need to predict capability breakthroughs. Since diffusion of new capabilities takes a long time, that gives us plenty of time to react — time that we often squander, and then panic! Watch the full argument here or read it below. Every week brings new claims about AI advances. How do we know what’s coming next? Could AI predict crime? Write award-winning novels? Hack into critical infrastructure?

items.title: Meta’s AI could still scrape news sites, legal experts say
items.raw_text: Meta has tweaked its business terms to remove language suggesting that it could freely train its AI models on news sites, like The Verge - but legal experts say these changes aren't enough to address their concerns. items.title: Meta turns Muse sharing back on
items.raw_text: Meta has re-enabled Muse sharing after security researchers had reported that public conversation links could be easy to find. Researchers at Claroc reported earlier this week that Muse the web addresses for shared conversations from Muse were named after a conversation's title and written into public DNS. items.title: The FCC is beginning to block gadgets with ‘foreign surveillance chips’
items.raw_text: On October 13th, Brendan Carr's FCC gave itself a new power - it can block gadgets for containing any computer chip made by any company on its list of potential threats to national security . Today, it's exercising that power for the first time, blocking two gadgets because they contain "foreign surveillance chips," the FCC claims . items.raw_text: Wachtwoordmanager 1Password komt met een functie waarmee AI-agents kunnen inloggen op gekoppelde accounts, zonder dat ze toegang krijgen tot de bijbehorende inloggegevens. Gebruikers moeten voor iedere inlogpoging wel eerst toestemming geven.

items.title: Arc Browser stopt per 22 december volledig
items.raw_text: The Browser Company stopt eind dit jaar met zijn Arc-webbrowser. Het bedrijf wil zich volledig richten op Dia, een andere webbrowser met een nadruk op AI. Vanaf 22 december is Arc niet meer te gebruiken, aldus het bedrijf.

items.title: Anthropic komt met Claude Duet-agent als antwoord op OpenAI Dots en Meta's Muse
items.raw_text: Anthropic komt met Claude Duet, een AI-agent die actief allerlei taken kan uitvoeren. Het bedrijf gaat daarmee de concurrentie aan met Meta's Muse-app en OpenAI's Dots. Claude Duet komt vooralsnog alleen als preview beschikbaar voor betalende gebruikers in de Verenigde Staten.

items.title: Fortinet brengt vandaag kritieke patches uit die klanten snel moeten installeren
items.raw_text: Fortinet brengt donderdag 22 oktober een reeks securityupdates uit voor zijn producten. Het raadt gebruikers met klem aan die patches meteen na release te installeren. De updates zijn voor verantwoord gemelde kwetsbaarheden, die mede met hulp van geavanceerde AI-modellen zijn gevonden.

items.title: OpenAI, Wiz en Calif werkten voor lek al maanden aan fix voor PHP-kwetsbaarheden
items.raw_text: Cybersecuritybedrijven Wiz, Calif en ChatGPT-aanbieder OpenAI werkten al twee maanden aan een oplossing voor de recente PHP-kwetsbaarheden. Informatie over die kwetsbaarheden lekte onlangs uit, waardoor wereldwijd talloze sites uit voorzorg offline gingen. Inmiddels is er een beveiligingsupdate voor de kwetsbaarheid.

items.title: Podcast De Dag: de kwetsbaarheid van PHP, 'de onderbroek' van het internet
items.raw_text: Van DigiD tot de Franse overheid, en van RTL Nieuws tot Schiphol. Sites van allerlei instanties gingen gisteren een paar uur offline. Er zaten lekken in PHP, een taal om sites te programmeren. Doordat die lekken op straat lagen, waren de sites kwetsbaar voor hackers. En dus was het veiliger om websites even uit de lucht te halen. Wat zegt dit lek over de kwetsbaarheid van ons internet? Luister hier: Deze aflevering van De Dag luister je via NPO Luister en alle andere podcastapps. Bevalt het? Vergeet je dan niet te abonneren. Volgens techjournalist van de NOS Joost Schellevis kan je PHP vergelijken met een onderbroek. Iedereen gebruikt het, het is belangrijk, maar normaal blijft het onzichtbaar. Met behulp van AI is het lek in die onderbroek nu gevonden. Kunstmatige intelligentie is een vloek en zegen voor de kwetsbaarheid van het internet. Aan de ene kant worden meer lekken gedicht die een mens moeilijk kan vinden. Aan de andere kant kunnen hackers die kwaad in de zin hebben, makkelijker toeslaan. Ook techsite Tweakers ging offline. Dat was jammer, want juist daar wilden ze over dit lek schrijven. Normaal gesproken wordt er pas over geschreven als de oplossing, een patch, voorhanden is. Maar nu ging die volgorde overhoop, waardoor het halve internet op zwart ging. Tweakers-hoofdredacteur Wout Funnekotter vreest dat dit niet de laatste keer zal zijn. Reageren: Mail naar dedag@nos.nl Presentatie & montage: Marco Geijtenbeek Redactie: Wouter Sloekers

items.title: Nog altijd websites niet bereikbaar na lek, ook internationaal nog problemen
items.raw_text: Er zijn nog altijd websites onbereikbaar nadat die uit voorzorg offline zijn gehaald. Dat gebeurde na een lek in de programmeertaal PHP. Zo is de website overheid.nl nog niet bereikbaar, evenals de site van Meld Misdaad Anoniem. De sites van 113 en Centrum Seksueel Geweld waren nog tot laat offline, maar die werden in de loop van de nacht weer bereikbaar. Een woordvoerder van het ministerie van Binnenlandse Zaken laat weten dat het nog niet duidelijk is wanneer overheid.nl weer beschikbaar komt. Sommige sites nemen langer de tijd om hun systemen te updaten en zijn daarom nog niet online. Ruim honderd gemeenten, provincies en waterschappen maken voor de verspreiding van officiële brieven gebruik van het raadssysteem Notubiz. De website van die organisatie is online, maar niet elk onderdeel is voor gemeenten of provincies te gebruiken. Officiële documenten van onder meer de gemeenten Den Haag, Almere, Breda, Haarlem, Den Bosch en Delft en van de provincies Overijssel, Gelderland en Friesland, kunnen niet worden ingezien. NotuBiz wil vanavond eerst testen of de updates goed zijn doorgevoerd en gaat ervan uit dat alle pagina's morgenochtend weer beschikbaar zijn. items.title: Zoveel sites in één klap plat: hoe kan dat? En zijn je gegevens veilig?
items.raw_text: Allerlei websites gaan uit voorzorg uit de lucht , van RTL Nieuws, DigiD en MijnOverheid tot de website van de Tweede Kamer. Wat is er precies aan de hand en waar komt dit grote beveiligingslek opeens vandaan? Hoe kwam dit lek aan het licht? Gisteren kwam de organisatie achter PHP, een programmeertaal waar veel websites uit zijn opgebouwd, met een aankondiging, zoals makers van software dat wel vaker doen: woensdag zou er een oplossing komen voor een probleem met PHP. Dat doen softwaremakers zodat iedereen zich kan voorbereiden op een oplossing. In dit geval hebben hackers die aankondiging echter aangegrepen om het precieze lek te lokaliseren en informatie erover naar buiten te brengen. Met die informatie is het relatief eenvoudig om het lek te misbruiken. Wat is PHP? PHP is een programmeertaal. Het is een van de oertalen van het wereldwijde web; de eerste versie kwam al in 1995 uit. Hoewel de populariteit is afgenomen doordat er nieuwe programmeertalen met een hipper imago verschenen, is het nog steeds een van de stille drijvende krachten achter het web. Liveblog Volg de laatste ontwikkelingen over het lek in ons liveblog . Het softwarelek van vandaag zit in de zogenoemde interpreter , een stukje software dat de door programmeurs geschreven commando's vertaalt naar iets wat de computer begrijpt. Hoe ernstig is dit lek? items.title: Opname-apparaatje ontdekt in vergaderzaal OpenAI, medewerker opgepakt
items.raw_text: AI-ontwikkelaar OpenAI heeft opname-apparatuur ontdekt in een van de eigen kantoren. Het Amerikaanse bedrijf spreekt van een "geavanceerd opname-apparaat". Het was geplaatst in een vergaderzaal in San Francisco waar vaak bedrijfsgevoelige informatie wordt besproken. OpenAI deed de ontdekking eind september. Het apparaatje was gewikkeld in wc-papier en zat in de usb-poort van een televisie. Daar zat het toen waarschijnlijk al twee dagen, zegt de FBI, die het onderzoek naar de kwestie leidt. Al snel leidde het spoor naar een Saudische werknemer van OpenAI. Die was te zien op camerabeelden bij de vergaderzaal, waar hij officieel geen toegang toe had. Ook zou de man (35) in de dagen ervoor opdrachten aan een AI-chatbot hebben gegeven die te maken hadden met het maken en opslaan van geluidsopnames. Verder is op camerabeelden te zien hoe de man achter de bewuste televisie naar iets lijkt te zoeken. Het opname-apparaatje was toen al ontdekt en verwijderd. Jarenlange celstraf dreigt De Saudische man is op 9 oktober opgepakt. Hij kan tot vijf jaar cel en een boete van maximaal 250.000 dollar krijgen. OpenAI heeft hem meteen op straat gezet. Het bedrijf zegt op X geen aanwijzingen te hebben dat hij waardevolle informatie in handen heeft gekregen. FBI-baas Kash Patel ziet in de zaak het bewijs dat het beschermen van Amerikaanse AI essentieel is voor de nationale veiligheid en economische voorspoed van het land. items.title: Ook ChatGPT-teksten krijgen onzichtbaar 'watermerk'
items.raw_text: Teksten van ChatGPT-gebruikers worden voorzien van een onzichtbaar 'watermerk'. Hiermee moet duidelijker worden of een tekst authentiek is of gegenereerd is door kunstmatige intelligentie, aldus OpenAI. Het watermerk, genaamd textGrain, wordt komende tijd verwerkt in AI-teksten van gebruikers in de Europese Unie. Daarbuiten bevatten de teksten geen watermerken. Het herkenningsteken is voor normale gebruikers niet te zien: het is namelijk geen fysiek stempel of speciaal teken, maar zit ingebouwd in de woordkeuzes van het generatieve AI-model. Korte teksten Een speciale detector kan dat watermerk, en daarmee door AI-gegenereerde woorden en teksten, wel oppikken. Die tool is vooralsnog alleen toegankelijk voor goedgekeurde onderzoekers en expertorganisaties, schrijft OpenAI. Het systeem is volgens het bedrijf achter ChatGPT sterk, maar niet foutloos, schrijft het bedrijf . Onder meer korte en bewerkte teksten maken betrouwbare detectie lastig. Anthropic, het bedrijf achter chatbot Claude, voerde twee maanden geleden een vergelijkbaar watermerk in: ook onzichtbaar voor mensenogen, maar wel waarneembaar voor computersystemen. Deze is wereldwijd toegepast. Concurrentie De bedrijven zeggen met hun watermerken de nieuwe Europese AI-transparantieregels te volgen. Een van die regels is dat content die door kunstmatige intelligentie is gemaakt een markering krijgt, zoals een watermerk . items.title: Tijdelijk verbod op AI-brillen in Noorwegen, regering stelt onderzoek in
items.raw_text: De Noorse regering wil een tijdelijk verbod op AI-brillen op een aantal plekken in de openbare ruimte. De regering zegt zich zorgen te maken dat mensen zonder hun medeweten kunnen worden gefilmd of gefotografeerd. Zo'n AI-bril lijkt op een gewone bril maar heeft een ingebouwde camera en microfoon. Ook is de bril voorzien van een AI-assistent. Het tijdelijk verbod geeft de regering "de tijd om grondig onderzoek te doen" voor het maken van regelgeving, zegt minister Micaelsen van Digitalisering. Het tijdelijk verbod zal gelden voor plekken die door een groot publiek worden bezocht. Het gaat om onder meer parken, winkelcentra en op plekken waar veel kinderen komen, zoals kinderdagverblijven en speeltuinen. Het verbod kan ook worden toegepast op privacygevoelige plekken, zoals ziekenhuizen en kleedkamers. Overwogen wordt of het verbod ook gaat gelden voor universiteiten en hogescholen. Onveilig De minister zegt dat mensen zich geen zorgen zouden moeten maken om stiekem opgenomen te worden op plekken en in situaties waar dat normaal gesproken ook niet gebeurt. "Zo'n samenleving kan als onveilig worden ervaren en ons ertoe aanzetten om ons terug te trekken", aldus Micaelsen. De Noorse regering onderzoekt voor welke technologische onderdelen het verbod precies zal gelden. Bijvoorbeeld of het verbod geldt voor brillen met camera en die geluid kunnen opnemen of voor brillen die kunnen opnemen en een AI-functie hebben. items.title: Britse supermarkten zetten AI in om stijgend aantal winkeldiefstallen te stoppen
items.raw_text: Een sterke stijging in winkeldiefstal maakt dat steeds meer Britse supermarkten en winkels beveiligingscamera's met AI-technologie en gezichtsherkenning installeren. "Als we dat niet doen, gaan we failliet", zegt Nathan Walmsley, de manager van supermarktketen Filco in Wales. "Zo extreem is het", vertelt hij. "Er wordt hier elke dag gestolen. Als we niet flink investeren in beveiliging, verliezen we simpelweg te veel geld aan diefstal om het hoofd boven water te houden." En hij is niet de enige. Door het hele land worden ondernemers geraakt door de toename van winkeldiefstal. Volgens de officiële cijfers gaat het om een half miljoen diefstalincidenten per jaar, maar de sector zelf schat het werkelijke aantal incidenten op twintig miljoen. "En dus moeten we het zelf oplossen." De supermarktketen in Wales heeft in alle filialen camera's geïnstalleerd die met AI-software 'verdachte' handelingen kunnen herkennen. In de video testen we het: Het werkt goed, zegt Walmsley. items.title: OpenAI pauzeert training modellen na aanval op overheidswebsites
items.raw_text: Het Amerikaanse bedrijf OpenAI heeft de training van zijn AI-modellen tijdelijk stopgezet. Aanleiding zijn de aanvallen van Open AI-agents afgelopen zomer op websites van onder meer de Amerikaanse overheid. AI-agents zijn AI-programma's die bepaalde opdrachten kunnen uitvoeren. De agents van OpenAI hadden geen opdracht gekregen om websites aan te vallen, dat deden ze om de taak te volbrengen die aan hen was gevraagd, werd gisteren bekendgemaakt door het non-profit AI-onderzoeksbureau Transluce. OpenAI zei in een reactie dat er geen sprake was van hacks, maar volgens The New York Times wisten de agents bij het ministerie van Handel informatie te vergaren door gebruik te maken van online gevonden login-gegevens. Andere AI-onderzoekers ontdekten dat OpenAI-agents actief waren op een Duits online forum. Ook dat was niet de bedoeling. OpenAI zegt dat de training alleen wordt hervat "als we er zeker van zijn dat we extra beveiligingsmaatregelen hebben". Het bedrijf verwacht dat het opnieuw op de pauzeknop moet drukken als AI zich verder ontwikkelt en zich nieuwe problemen voordoen. items.title: Besi overtreft verwachtingen met sterke ordergroei dankzij ai-boom
items.raw_text: BE Semiconductor Industries (Besi) verwacht dat de vraag naar zijn chipmachines dit kwartaal verder aanzwelt, nu de uitbreiding van ai-capaciteit onverminderd doorgaat. Over het afgelopen kwartaal meldt de chipmachinefabrikant uit Duiven een sterke instroom van nieuwe orders. Het order-volume van Besi steeg met 342,6 miljoen euro, veel meer dan de 298 miljoen euro waarop de markt rekende. Zo blijkt uit de kwartaalcijfers die Besi donderdag publiceerde. Vergeleken met het kwartaal daarvoor lag het orderniveau 17 procent hoger. Ten opzichte van dezelfde periode een jaar eerder bedroeg de stijging zelfs 96 procent. Dit kwam vooral door een toename in orders voor ‘hybrid bonding’, datacenter-oplossingen en ai-gerelateerde computertoepassingen, waaronder systemen voor energiebeheer. Het totale order-volume van Besi over de afgelopen twaalf maanden steeg naar 1,2 miljard euro. Hybrid bonding Desondanks daalde de koers van Besi op donderdag. En sinds juni is het aandeel ongeveer gehalveerd. Volgens Jean-Paul van Oudheusden, marktanalist bij eToro, twijfelen beleggers vooral aan de groei op lange termijn. ‘De verrassend hoge orderinstroom laat zien dat Besi voorlopig volop profiteert van de ai-investeringsgolf. items.title: Ot-beveiliging: spaghetti moet lasagne worden
items.raw_text: De systemen die onze fabrieken, gebouwen en energievoorzieningen aansturen, zijn steeds vaker digitaal verbonden en daardoor kwetsbaar. Organisaties beveiligen hun it systemen en bedrijfsgegevens, maar operationele technologie (ot) krijgt onvoldoende aandacht. Het overzicht ontbreekt en structureel risicobeheer is ondermaats. Het gevolg: productieprocessen vallen stil, logistieke stromen raken verstoord en zelfs onze energievoorziening kan worden geraakt. Hoe kwetsbaar die systemen kunnen zijn, bleek onlangs uit onderzoek naar Europese windparken en zonneparken. Onderzoekers ontdekten ruim 8.500 beheersystemen die via internet bereikbaar waren, waarvan 141 in Nederland. Bij sommige installaties was zelfs bediening op afstand mogelijk. Het onderzoek legt een veel breder probleem bloot: bedrijven verbinden steeds meer operationele systemen met het internet, zonder dat de digitale veiligheid altijd voldoende wordt meegenomen. Achterhaalde organisatiestructuren Die blinde vlek heeft een historische verklaring. Operationele technologie functioneerde lange tijd grotendeels zelfstandig. De verantwoordelijkheid lag bij technische of facilitaire afdelingen, terwijl it zich richtte op de digitale kantooromgeving en informatiebeveiliging. Inmiddels zijn die werelden steeds verder met elkaar verweven, maar de organisatiestructuren zijn nauwelijks mee veranderd. Vooral de energietransitie versnelt die ontwikkeling.
